claim: Fundc1 knockout mice (F1KO) are grossly normal and fertile.
source: Mice with germline knockout of Fundc1 (F1KO) are grossly normal and fertile.
evidence: Direct statement in the Results section describing the phenotype of F1KO mice

claim: F1KO mice have a normal blood count and spleen size.
source: They have a normal blood count and spleen size (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Hypoxia (8% oxygen for 72 hr) reduces mitochondrial protein levels (Tom20, COXII, Tim23) in wild-type mouse tissues.
source: Levels of mitochondrial proteins and P62 were reduced in response to hypoxia in tissues isolated from WT mice, although the degree of degradation differs in different tissues.
evidence: Western blot data showing reduced mitochondrial protein levels in WT tissues after hypoxia

claim: Hypoxia-induced degradation of mitochondrial proteins is blocked in F1KO mice.
source: Degradation of these proteins was blocked in F1KO mice.
evidence: Western blot data comparing WT and F1KO mice under hypoxia

claim: LC3-II levels are significantly increased in hypoxic wild-type tissues.
source: LC3-II levels were significantly increased in hypoxic wild-type tissues, whereas LC3-I levels were maintained in F1KO tissues under the same conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 showing LC3-II accumulation

claim: Prolonged hypoxia strongly depletes mitochondrial proteins in platelets from WT but not F1KO mice.
source: Prolonged hypoxia strongly depleted mitochondrial proteins and other mitophagy marker proteins in platelets isolated from WT but not F1KO mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 1A showing differential effects in WT vs F1KO platelets

claim: ER marker calnexin and Golgi marker GM130 show little change under hypoxia in platelets.
source: Under similar conditions, the ER marker calnexin and the Golgi marker GM130 showed little change (Figure 1A).
evidence: Western blot data showing stable levels of ER and Golgi markers

claim: FUNDC1 becomes dephosphorylated at Tyr18 under hypoxic conditions.
source: FUNDC1 is normally phosphorylated at Tyr18 by Src kinase and becomes dephosphorylated under hypoxic conditions, thus increasing its affinity with LC3 for the activation of mitophagy.
evidence: Western blot data showing loss of p-18-FUNDC1 signal under hypoxia

claim: Transmission electron microscopy reveals mitochondria enclosed within double-membrane autophagic structures in hypoxic WT platelets.
source: Transmission electron microscopy also revealed a mitochondrion enclosed within a double-membrane autophagic membrane in platelets isolated from hypoxic WT mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Electron microscopy images in Figure 1B showing mitophagosomes

claim: Mitophagosomes were not observed in platelets from hypoxic F1KO mice.
source: However, mitophagosomes were not observed in platelets from hypoxic F1KO mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Electron microscopy data showing absence of mitophagosomes in F1KO platelets

claim: 6 out of 485 mitochondria were observed within autophagosomes in 97 platelets from WT mice exposed to hypoxia (8% O2) for 72 hr.
source: Quantification of mitochondria enclosed in autophagosomes was performed, and 6 out of 485 mitochondria were observed within autophagosomes in 97 platelets from WT mice exposed to hypoxia (8% O2) for 72 hr.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of electron microscopy images

claim: FUNDC1 strongly interacts with LC3 in platelets isolated from WT mice exposed to hypoxia for 72 hr.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (CO-IP) analysis revealed that FUNDC1 strongly interacted with LC3 in platelets isolated from WT mice exposed to hypoxia for 72 hr.
evidence: Co-IP data showing FUNDC1-LC3 interaction under hypoxia

claim: Little FUNDC1-LC3 interaction was detected in platelets from untreated WT mice.
source: Little interaction was detected in platelets from untreated WT mice, and no interaction was detected in the platelets from treated or untreated F1KO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Co-IP data showing minimal interaction in normoxic WT platelets

claim: No FUNDC1-LC3 interaction was detected in platelets from F1KO mice under hypoxia or normoxia.
source: Little interaction was detected in platelets from untreated WT mice, and no interaction was detected in the platelets from treated or untreated F1KO mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Co-IP data showing absence of interaction in F1KO platelets

claim: Ex vivo hypoxia or FCCP treatment of platelets induces mitophagy phenotypes similar to in vivo treatment.
source: As expected, ex vivo assays in which platelets were isolated and then treated with hypoxia or FCCP, a commonly used inducer of mitophagy, showed almost identical mitophagy phenotypes to those in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,B).
evidence: Western blot and EM data comparing in vivo and ex vivo treatments

claim: Platelet-specific knockout of Fundc1 (Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+) blocks hypoxia-induced mitophagy in platelets.
source: platelets from Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice, but not Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice, showed an increase in LC3-II levels and a decrease in Tim23, Tom20 and P62 levels.
evidence: Western blot data from platelet-specific Fundc1 knockout mice

claim: Biochemical mitophagic hallmarks were evident in leukocytes from both Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- and Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice.
source: In contrast, biochemical mitophagic hallmarks were evident in leukocytes from both Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- and Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice (unpublished observation).
evidence: Statement indicating tissue-specific effect of platelet-specific knockout

claim: Atg5 is required for FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy.
source: We previously showed that Atg5, the master regulator for general autophagy, is also required for FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: Reference to previous publication

claim: Platelet-specific deletion of Atg5 blocks hypoxia-induced mitophagy in platelets.
source: Hypoxia failed to activate platelet mitophagy in the absence of Atg5, as revealed by examination of mitophagy marker proteins (Figure 1F,and Figure 1—figure supplement 5)
evidence: Western blot data from Atg5fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice

claim: Maximum mitochondrial oxidative capacity is markedly decreased in F1KO platelets.
source: Seahorse analysis revealed that both the maximum mitochondrial oxidative capacity and the basal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate were markedly decreased in F1KO platelets (Figure 2A).
evidence: Seahorse metabolic analysis data

claim: Basal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate is markedly decreased in F1KO platelets.
source: Seahorse analysis revealed that both the maximum mitochondrial oxidative capacity and the basal mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate were markedly decreased in F1KO platelets (Figure 2A).
evidence: Seahorse metabolic analysis data

claim: Hypoxic treatment induces significant reduction in oxygen consumption in WT platelets but has little effect on F1KO platelets.
source: Consistent with our discovery that extensive mitochondrial protein degradation is prevented in F1KO platelets, we found that hypoxic treatments induced significant reduction in oxygen consumption in WT platelets, while it had little effect on platelets from F1KO mice (Figure 2A).
evidence: Seahorse data comparing WT and F1KO platelets under hypoxia

claim: ATP production is impaired in F1KO platelets.
source: Similarly, ATP production was impaired in F1KO platelets, and was also significantly reduced in hypoxia-treated WT platelets compared to untreated WT platelets (Figure 2B).
evidence: ATP measurement data

claim: Mitochondrial mass is markedly increased in F1KO platelets.
source: The reduced mitochondrial activities in F1KO platelets are likely due to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria owing to defective mitophagy, as mitochondrial mass and ROS were markedly increased in F1KO platelets whereas mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly decreased (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring mitochondrial mass with NAO staining

claim: ROS levels are markedly increased in F1KO platelets.
source: The reduced mitochondrial activities in F1KO platelets are likely due to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria owing to defective mitophagy, as mitochondrial mass and ROS were markedly increased in F1KO platelets whereas mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly decreased (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring ROS with DCF

claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is significantly decreased in F1KO platelets.
source: The reduced mitochondrial activities in F1KO platelets are likely due to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria owing to defective mitophagy, as mitochondrial mass and ROS were markedly increased in F1KO platelets whereas mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly decreased (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring membrane potential with TMRE

claim: FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy determines the quality and functional integrity of mitochondria in platelets.
source: These data demonstrate that FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy determines the quality and functional integrity of mitochondria in platelets.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental results

claim: Exposure of WT mice to hypoxia significantly reduces platelet aggregation upon treatment with thrombin.
source: Exposure of WT mice to hypoxia significantly reduced platelet aggregation, platelet spreading and surface expression of P-selectin upon treatment with thrombin (Figure 2F,H,I)
evidence: Platelet aggregation assay data

claim: Aggregation of platelets from F1KO mice is markedly reduced in response to thrombin.
source: In contrast, aggregation of platelets from F1KO mice was markedly reduced in response to thrombin (Figure 2F,H,I).
evidence: Platelet aggregation assay data

claim: Mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate is closely related to the level of platelet aggregation with a correlation coefficient close to one in WT platelets.
source: Mitochondrial activity, represented by mitochondrial oxygen consumption rates, was closely related to the level of platelet aggregation, with a correlation coefficient close to one in platelets from WT, Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- and Atg5fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice (Figure 2G,K,O).
evidence: Correlation analysis between OCR and aggregation

claim: Platelet activation is compromised in F1KO, Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ and Atg5fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ platelets and is not further reduced by hypoxia.
source: In contrast, platelet activation was compromised in F1KO platelets, Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ and Atg5fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ platelets, and was not further reduced by hypoxia (Figure 2).
evidence: Platelet activation assay data from multiple knockout models

claim: There is no significant change in the levels of ADP receptor P2Y12 and thrombin receptors (PARs) in F1KO platelets.
source: This is also a specific effect, because there was no significant change in the levels of the ADP receptor P2Y12 and the thrombin receptors (PARs), and downstream signaling mediated by the platelet integrin receptor IIbIIIa (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–G).
evidence: Western blot and flow cytometry data showing receptor levels

claim: Megakaryocyte differentiation is identical in WT and F1KO mice.
source: Megakaryocyte differentiation was also identical in WT and F1KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis of bone marrow

claim: Deficiency of Fundc1 does not enhance apoptosis in platelets in response to ABT737 (10 μM).
source: Deficiency of Fundc1 did not enhance apoptosis in platelets in response to ABT737 (10 μM) under our experimental conditions, as measured by phosphatidylserine (PS) exposure and activation of caspase-3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Flow cytometry and caspase activity assay data

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of unphosphorylated peptide P, but not phosphorylated peptide C, blocks hypoxia-induced mitochondrial protein degradation in WT platelets.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of the unphosphorylated peptide (P), but not the phosphorylated peptide which was used as a control (C), effectively blocked hypoxia-induced mitochondrial protein and P62 degradation and the conversion of LC3-I into LC3-II in WT platelets (Figure 3A).
evidence: Western blot data from peptide-treated mice

claim: Neither peptide P nor C has any effect on mitophagy in F1KO platelets.
source: Neither peptide had any effect in F1KO platelets (Figure 3A).
evidence: Western blot data showing no effect of peptides in F1KO platelets

claim: Peptide P, but not peptide C, inhibits the FUNDC1/LC3 interaction in WT platelets under hypoxic conditions.
source: CO-IP results demonstrated that peptide P, but not peptide C, inhibited the FUNDC1/LC3 interaction in WT platelets under hypoxic conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Co-IP data showing disruption of FUNDC1-LC3 interaction by peptide P

claim: Peptide P, but not C, effectively blocks the hypoxia-induced decrease in oxygen consumption rate in WT platelets.
source: Importantly, peptide P, but not C, effectively blocked the hypoxia-induced decrease in oxygen consumption rate and ATP generation in WT platelets (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: Seahorse and ATP measurement data

claim: Peptide P prevents the loss of mitochondrial mass in hypoxic WT platelets.
source: Also, peptide P, but not C, prevented the loss of mitochondrial mass, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and the increase of ROS in hypoxic WT platelets (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Flow cytometry data measuring mitochondrial parameters

claim: Peptide P significantly prevents the reduction of platelet aggregation upon exposure to hypoxia in WT platelets.
source: As expected, peptide P, but not C, significantly prevented the reduction of platelet aggregation, platelet spreading and surface expression of P-selectin upon exposure to hypoxia for 72 hr in WT platelets (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: Platelet aggregation and activation assay data

claim: Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice have much smaller heart infarct size (IF/AAR) than Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice after I/R.
source: Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice had much smaller heart infarct size (IF/AAR) than Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice as revealed by the 2, 3, 5 - triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining assay, and there was no significant difference in area at risk/left ventricle (AAR/LV) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: TTC staining and quantification of infarct size

claim: There is no significant difference in area at risk/left ventricle (AAR/LV) between Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ and Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice after I/R.
source: Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice had much smaller heart infarct size (IF/AAR) than Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice as revealed by the 2, 3, 5 - triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) staining assay, and there was no significant difference in area at risk/left ventricle (AAR/LV) (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: TTC staining and quantification data

claim: Myocardial functions in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice are normal under normoxic conditions.
source: Echocardiography analysis showed that myocardial functions in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice are normal under normoxic conditions, because the basal levels of fractional shortening (FS) and ejection fraction (EF) are comparable to those in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Echocardiography data comparing baseline cardiac function

claim: Following I/R, Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice show a significant reduction in myocardial functions compared to Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice.
source: Following I/R, Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice showed a significant reduction in myocardial functions, as measured by FS and EF, compared to Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: Echocardiography data after I/R injury

claim: P-selectin surface expression is induced following I/R in hearts.
source: In agreement with early platelet activation as reported previously, we found that P-selectin surface expression was induced following I/R in hearts.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data showing P-selectin expression

claim: P-selectin surface expression is significantly higher in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice than in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice during I/R.
source: Also, consistent with the high degree of heart injury, P-selectin surface expression was significantly higher in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice than that in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice during I/R (Figure 4H,M).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data

claim: I/R treatment significantly reduces blood oxygen saturation levels.
source: Indeed, blood oxygen saturation measurements revealed that I/R treatment significantly reduced the oxygen saturation levels (Figure 4I).
evidence: Blood oxygen saturation measurement data

claim: Platelet mitophagy occurs in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice within 24 hr of I/R.
source: Western blotting analysis revealed that platelet mitophagy occurred in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice within 24 hr of I/R, and it was blocked in Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre+ mice (Figure 4J).
evidence: Western blot data showing mitophagy markers over time

claim: Mitochondrial OCR and ATP levels are both significantly reduced in platelets from Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice after I/R.
source: Correspondingly, mitochondrial OCR and ATP levels were both significantly reduced in platelets from Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice after I/R (Figure 4K,L).
evidence: Seahorse and ATP measurement data

claim: Both surface expression level of P-selectin and aggregation level of platelets from Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- progressively decline as reperfusion time increases.
source: At later time points, both the surface expression level of P-selectin and the aggregation level of platelets isolated from Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- progressively declined compared to sham controls as the reperfusion time increased (Figure 4M,N).
evidence: Flow cytometry and aggregation data over time course

claim: Hypoxic preconditioning of Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice strongly blocks I/R-induced heart injury.
source: Hypoxic preconditioning of the Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice strongly blocked I/R-induced heart injury (Figure 5B,C), and this was reversed by the administration of peptide P, but not the control peptide C.
evidence: TTC staining and infarct size quantification data

claim: The protective effect of hypoxic preconditioning on heart injury is reversed by peptide P but not peptide C.
source: Hypoxic preconditioning of the Fundc1fl/fl::Pf4Cre- mice strongly blocked I/R-induced heart injury (Figure 5B,C), and this was reversed by the administration of peptide P, but not the control peptide C.
evidence: TTC staining data comparing peptide treatments

claim: Hypoxic preconditioning maintains heart functions as evaluated by FS and EF, and this protective effect is reduced by peptide P but not peptide C.
source: Likewise, hypoxic preconditioning maintained heart functions, as evaluated by FS and EF, and this protective effect was reduced by peptide P, but not peptide C (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Echocardiography data from preconditioned mice

claim: Hypoxic preconditioning prevents P-selectin surface expression in platelets under I/R, and this is reversed by peptide P but not peptide C.
source: Indeed, hypoxic preconditioning prevented P-selectin surface expression in platelets under I/R (Figure 5F), and this was reversed by peptide P, but not peptide C.
evidence: Immunohistochemistry and flow cytometry data

claim: Peptide P, but not C, prevents hypoxic and I/R-induced mitophagy in platelets.
source: Biochemical analysis revealed that peptide P, but not C, prevented hypoxic and I/R-induced mitophagy (Figure 5K).
evidence: Western blot data showing mitophagy markers

claim: Hypoxic mitophagy in platelets is a key component of the protective effect of hypoxic preconditioning on I/R-induced heart injury.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrated that hypoxic mitophagy in platelets is a key component of the protective effect of hypoxic preconditioning on I/R-induced heart injury.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental results

claim: Mitophagy regulates mitochondrial quality control and mediates mitochondrial degradation in (patho-)physiological settings.
source: Here we demonstrated that mitophagy regulates mitochondrial quality control and mediates mitochondrial degradation in (patho-)physiological settings.
evidence: Summary statement in Discussion section

claim: Hypoxic mitophagy dictates the level of mitochondrial activity, which is related to the level of platelet activity.
source: We also showed that hypoxic mitophagy dictates the level of mitochondrial activity, which is related to the level of platelet activity.
evidence: Summary statement based on correlation data

claim: Administration of the unphosphorylated peptide prevents extensive mitophagy under prolonged hypoxic conditions, thus blocking mitochondrial depletion and platelet inactivation.
source: Administration of the unphosphorylated peptide prevents extensive mitophagy under prolonged hypoxic conditions, thus blocking mitochondrial depletion and platelet inactivation.
evidence: Summary of peptide treatment effects

claim: Loss of FUNDC1 results in compromised mitochondrial functions and reduces platelet activity to a low but constant level which is insensitive to hypoxia or peptides.
source: In contrast, loss of FUNDC1 results in compromised mitochondrial functions and reduces platelet activity to a low but constant level which is insensitive to hypoxia or peptides.
evidence: Summary of F1KO phenotype

claim: FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy regulates mitochondrial quality and quantity in both normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
source: Taking advantage of the unique platelet system, we clearly showed that FUNDC1-mediated mitophagy regulates mitochondrial quality and quantity in both normoxic and in hypoxic conditions.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple experimental results

claim: Platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have increased mitochondrial mass under normoxic conditions.
source: It appears that platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have increased mitochondrial mass (Figure 2), decreased mitochondrial function (Figure 2) and reduced platelet activation (Figure 3) even under normoxic conditions
evidence: Flow cytometry data showing mitochondrial mass

claim: Platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have decreased mitochondrial function under normoxic conditions.
source: It appears that platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have increased mitochondrial mass (Figure 2), decreased mitochondrial function (Figure 2) and reduced platelet activation (Figure 3) even under normoxic conditions
evidence: Seahorse and ATP data

claim: Platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have reduced platelet activation under normoxic conditions.
source: It appears that platelets in FUNDC1 knockout mice have increased mitochondrial mass (Figure 2), decreased mitochondrial function (Figure 2) and reduced platelet activation (Figure 3) even under normoxic conditions
evidence: Platelet aggregation and activation assay data

claim: There is a tissue-specific effect of mitophagy in response to hypoxia.
source: These data suggest that there is a tissue-specific effect of mitophagy in response to hypoxia, and this is likely due to distinct mechanisms for balancing mitophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis in the hypoxic stress response.
evidence: Comparison of mitophagy in different tissues

claim: Platelet mitophagy has dual roles in platelet activation and in I/R injury.
source: It is interesting to note that platelet mitophagy has dual roles in platelet activation and in I/R injury.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental observations

claim: In the acute phase, mitophagy maintains mitochondrial quality and function by removing damaged mitochondria to support platelet activation.
source: In the acute phase, mitophagy maintains mitochondrial quality and function by getting rid of damaged mitochondria that are 'toxic', so as to support platelet activation.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental results

claim: In the prolonged phase, extensive elimination of mitochondria due to hypoxia renders platelets less active, preventing excess I/R-induced injury.
source: In the prolonged phase, extensive elimination of mitochondria (maybe even good-quality and partially functional ones) due to hypoxia renders the platelets less active, preventing excess I/R-induced injury.
evidence: Interpretation of time-course experimental data

claim: Hypoxic mitophagy in platelets is causally linked with I/R-induced heart injury.
source: We thus revealed that hypoxic mitophagy in platelets is causally linked with I/R-induced heart injury, and that mitophagy in platelets plays a dual role in the I/R injury of hearts.
evidence: Summary statement based on I/R experimental results

claim: Hypoxic preconditioning induces extensive mitochondrial degradation and drastic inactivation of platelet activity, thus preventing I/R injury.
source: We have shown that hypoxic preconditioning induces extensive mitochondrial degradation and drastic inactivation of platelet activity, thus preventing I/R injury.
evidence: Summary of preconditioning experimental results

claim: Preconditioning agents affect oxygen levels in the blood or heart, thus activating mitophagy in platelets to reduce platelet activation and I/R injury.
source: These preconditioning agents affect oxygen levels in the blood or in the heart (Fullmer et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2015), thus activating mitophagy in platelets to reduce platelet activation and I/R injury.
evidence: Interpretation based on experimental results and cited literature

claim: Mitophagy occurs in platelets from patients with hypoxemia and myocardial infarction.
source: This is of clinical significance and our preliminary clinical studies have shown that mitophagy in platelets occurs in patients with hypoxemia and myocardial infarction (unpublished observations).
evidence: Reference to unpublished clinical observations

claim: Administration of peptide P is the first plausible method for manipulating mitophagy in vivo.
source: Administration of peptide P is the first plausible method for manipulating mitophagy in vivo and fighting IR-induced heart injury.
evidence: Summary statement based on peptide experiments

claim: Targeting mitophagy in both cardiomyocytes and platelets will offer new life-saving strategies for fighting clinical complications.
source: Therefore, targeting mitophagy both in cardiomyocytes (Dorn et al., 2015) and platelets (Figure 5) or reducing mitochondrial activity by pharmacological and biochemical means will offer new life-saving strategies for fighting these deadly clinical complications.
evidence: Concluding statement based on experimental results and cited literature

claim: FUNDC1 localizes at the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: In addition to Parkin/PINK1 which mediates mitophagy in response to loss of mitochondrial membrane potential and acute stresses (Lazarou et al., 2015), several mitophagy receptors, including FUNDC1, localize at the outer mitochondrial membrane (Novak et al., 2010; Zhang and Ney, 2010; Liu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; Wu et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations

claim: Mitophagy receptors interact with LC3 via a LIR motif to initiate mitophagy.
source: These receptors interact with LC3 (ATG8 in yeast) via a LIR (LC3-interacting region) motif to initiate mitophagy (Okamoto et al., 2009; Kanki and Klionsky, 2010).
evidence: Statement supported by citations

claim: PINK1 phosphorylates Parkin to trigger selective autophagy of unwanted and damaged mitochondria.
source: PINK1 phosphorylates the E3 ubiquitin ligase Parkin to trigger selective autophagy of unwanted and damaged mitochondria (Lazarou et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citation

claim: In response to hypoxia, FUNDC1 is dephosphorylated, thus enhancing the FUNDC1/LC3 interaction.
source: In response to hypoxia, FUNDC1 is dephosphorylated, thus enhancing the FUNDC1/LC3 interaction (Liu et al., 2012), while BNIP3 and NIX are transcriptionally upregulated (Kane et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations

claim: Ablation of NIX impairs mitochondrial clearance during red blood cell differentiation, causing a failure of erythroid maturation.
source: Ablation of NIX impairs mitochondrial clearance during red blood cell differentiation, causing a failure of erythroid maturation (Regula et al., 2002; Diwan et al., 2007; Sandoval et al., 2008; Ney, 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations

claim: Mitochondrial distribution and morphology in Bnip3/Nix double knockout hearts are markedly perturbed.
source: Mitochondrial distribution and morphology in Bnip3/Nix double knockout hearts were markedly perturbed (Dorn, 2010)
evidence: Statement supported by citation

claim: Parkin-mediated mitophagy is important for adapting to acute stress in the myocardium.
source: Parkin-mediated mitophagy is also important for adapting to acute stress (Kubli et al., 2013) in the myocardium, although it may not be essential for normal turnover of cardiac mitochondria (Kubli et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation

claim: Pink1−/− mice develop pathological cardiac hypertrophy accompanied by impaired mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes.
source: Pink1−/− mice develop pathological cardiac hypertrophy (Youle and Strasser, 2008; Billia et al., 2011) accompanied by an impaired mitochondrial function in cardiomyocytes.
evidence: Statement supported by citations

claim: Circulating platelets are specialized anucleate blood cells that contain small numbers of fully functional mitochondria.
source: Circulating platelets are specialized anucleate blood cells that contain small numbers of fully functional mitochondria (Zharikov and Shiva, 2013).
evidence: Statement supported by citation

claim: Platelet activation is highly energy-dependent and relies heavily on fully functional mitochondria.
source: Thus, platelet activation is highly energy-dependent and relies heavily on fully functional mitochondria (Kramer et al., 2014; Garcia-Souza and Oliveira, 2014).
evidence: Statement supported by citations

claim: General autophagy occurs in platelets in response to starvation in an ATG5-dependent fashion.
source: General autophagy occurs in platelets in response to starvation in an ATG5-dependent fashion (Lee et al., 2016; Feng et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2015; Ouseph et al., 2015)
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations

claim: A recent report suggests that mitophagy in diabetic platelets protects against severe oxidative stress.
source: A recent report suggests that mitophagy in diabetic platelets protects against severe oxidative stress (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement supported by citation

claim: Platelet activation is a major pathophysiological mechanism underlying atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, acute coronary syndromes and I/R-related damage.
source: Platelet activation is a major (patho-)physiological mechanism that underlies atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction acute coronary syndromes and ischemia/reperfusion (I/R)-related damage, and thus anti-platelet therapy is important for managing many cardiovascular diseases (Nagareddy and Smyth, 2013; Gawaz et al., 2005; Antithrombotic Trialists' Collaboration, 2002; Du, 2007; Ruggeri, 2002; Li et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations
